transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, thank you. Um… what finally pushed me to make the appointment is that I’m having a really hard time staying with things that I genuinely need to focus on at work. I manage in a medical setting, so I’m often looking at EPIC quality reports or sitting in clinic metrics meetings, and I go in with every intention of following the numbers and tracking what’s being said.

But within a few minutes, it’s like my mind has wandered somewhere else without me even noticing it happened. Then I’ll look back at the report and realize I’ve been rereading the same line or the same set of numbers over and over, and I still don’t really know what I just read. Or in a meeting, someone will ask a follow-up or the discussion will move on, and I realize I missed the whole point of what was just being discussed.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because these are things I know how to do and care about doing well. It’s not that I don’t understand the material — it’s more that I can’t seem to keep my attention anchored to it long enough. That’s really what made me think, okay, I probably need to talk to someone about this.
Have you noticed that you feel restless or have trouble staying still during these times when you're struggling to focus?

I’m not sure I’d describe it as restlessness, exactly. I don’t really notice myself needing to get up and move around or feeling like I physically can’t stay in the chair. At least, that’s not the main thing I’m aware of.

It’s more internal, I guess—like I’m sitting there, appearing still, but my attention has slipped away. I might shift in my seat or adjust my posture, but I think most people do that. I haven’t really connected it with the focus issue in a way where I’d say, “Yes, I’m restless.” So… no, not that I’ve clearly noticed.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, especially around the times when you're struggling with focus?

I don’t think so, at least not in a clear way. I mean, I do get frustrated with myself when it happens, especially if I’ve just missed something in a meeting or I’m sitting there thinking, “Why can’t I just follow this like everyone else seems to?” But I wouldn’t say I feel hopeless, exactly.

And I don’t think I’ve lost interest in things I usually enjoy. It’s more that during those moments I feel annoyed or embarrassed, maybe a little drained afterward because I’m trying so hard to catch up mentally. But it doesn’t feel like the focus problems are happening because I’m sad, if that makes sense. It feels more like the focus goes first, and then I feel bad about the fact that I lost track.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot or feeling anxious, especially when you're trying to focus, even if you're not sure what you're worried about?

I’m not sure I would call it anxiety, exactly. I mean, I do sometimes feel tense once I realize I’ve lost the thread, because then I’m trying to quickly catch up and not look like I missed something important. So there’s a bit of pressure in that moment.

But I don’t think I’m sitting there worrying a lot beforehand, like having a specific fear or a general anxious feeling that’s causing the focus problem. It’s more like I’m trying to focus, my mind drifts, and then I feel stressed because I notice it happened. If that distinction makes sense. I don’t usually have a sense of, “I’m anxious and that’s why I can’t concentrate.” It feels more like the concentration just… slips away, and then I react to that.
Have there been times when you feel like you're not fully present or aware of what's going on around you, almost like you're 'zoning out' or detached from yourself or your surroundings?

Yes, I think “zoning out” is actually a pretty good way to put it, though I don’t know if I’d say I feel detached from myself exactly. It’s more like I’m physically there and I look like I’m listening or working, but my mind has gone somewhere else without me really choosing that.

What finally pushed me to come in was that I’ll sit down to start an EPIC quality report, or I’ll be in a clinic metrics meeting fully intending to track what’s being discussed, and then within a few minutes I realize I’m not actually with it anymore. Like I’ll be staring at the same set of numbers and rereading them over and over, but they’re not really landing. Or someone will be talking through a metric or a workflow issue, and then suddenly I realize I missed the whole point of what they just said.

It’s embarrassing because I’m not trying to tune out. I go in thinking, “Okay, pay attention, this matters,” and then it’s like I come back online and have to piece together what happened from context. So yes, in that sense, I do feel not fully present at times—but more like my attention drifts away than like I’m outside my body or anything like that.
When you say your mind has gone somewhere else, do you ever feel disconnected from your body or like you're watching yourself from the outside, even briefly?

No, I don’t think so. Not like watching myself from the outside or feeling separated from my body. I’m trying to think if there’s ever been even a brief moment like that, but that doesn’t really sound familiar to me.

When I say my mind goes somewhere else, I mean it more in the everyday sense of zoning out—like my attention has wandered and I didn’t catch what was happening. I’m still aware that I’m sitting in the meeting room or at my desk, and I don’t feel unreal or like I’m looking at myself from across the room or anything like that.

It’s more like I’m there, but not processing. Like the information is happening in front of me and somehow I’m not taking it in. Then I notice and feel that little jolt of, “Oh no, what did I miss?” But I still feel like me, in my body, in the room. Just… not mentally tracking the way I meant to.
Do you often have trouble finishing tasks that require sustained mental effort, like reports or meetings, even if they’re important or something you care about?

Yes, definitely. That’s actually one of the main things that’s been bothering me at work, because these aren’t optional or unimportant tasks. They’re usually exactly the kind of things I know need to get done.

A typical example would be after a committee meeting. Someone will give me three or four follow-up steps—like send an email to this person, update a spreadsheet, draft a summary, and then submit something final. And I’ll leave the meeting with every intention of doing all of it. I may even start right away, which is the frustrating part. I’ll do the first step, maybe draft part of the second thing, and then somehow the rest just… stalls.

It’s not that I decided not to do it, and it’s not that I don’t care. It’s more like the email sits in drafts, or the spreadsheet is open but not finished, or the final submission is technically almost done but not actually sent. And then it just stays there until someone reminds me or asks about it, and then I feel awful because I really did mean to follow through. It’s embarrassing, especially because these are professional responsibilities and I know people are counting on me.
Looking back, did you have similar struggles with staying focused or finishing tasks when you were younger, like in school or when doing homework?

Yes, looking back, I think it was there pretty early, even in elementary school. I didn’t think of it that way at the time, of course—I just remember being told I was smart but that I was “careless” or not applying myself. Teachers would write things like that on report cards, that I was bright but made careless mistakes, or that I needed to pay closer attention.

And homework was a whole thing at home. My mother really had to sit with me a lot of the time to get me through it, not because I couldn’t understand it, but because I would lose track of what I was supposed to be doing. I’d forget which assignments were due, or I’d leave the book I needed at school and only realize it once I was home. Then there would be this whole scramble or frustration around trying to finish something that should have been straightforward.

I can remember feeling embarrassed because I knew I wasn’t stupid, and I don’t think my teachers thought I was either. It was more like I kept missing steps or failing to bring home the right materials, and then everyone would be frustrated with me because it looked careless. So yes, it does feel like this pattern goes way back, not just something that started with my current job.

Do you often feel like you need to be doing something all the time, or find it hard to wait your turn, like you jump in before people are done talking or make decisions quickly without thinking them through?

I’m not sure I’d describe myself that way, no. I don’t really feel like I have to be moving or doing something constantly. If anything, I can sit still for a long time—probably too long sometimes—especially if I’m sort of stuck or trying to get myself to start something.

With waiting my turn or interrupting, I don’t think that’s a major issue for me. I mean, I’m sure I’ve accidentally talked over someone here or there like anyone does, especially in a busy meeting, but I don’t think people would describe me as someone who’s always jumping in or unable to wait. I’m usually more worried about losing my train of thought or trying to make sure I say the right thing, so I may hold back rather than blurt things out.

And with decisions, I don’t think I’m especially impulsive in the sense of making big choices without thinking. If anything, I can overthink things. So no, the “need to be doing something all the time” or “can’t wait my turn” piece doesn’t really feel like it fits me very strongly.
Do you find that tasks requiring sustained attention leave you feeling mentally drained or exhausted, even if they aren’t physically demanding?

Yes, very much so. It’s actually hard to explain because it’s not like I’m physically doing anything strenuous, but certain tasks feel exhausting before I even start them.

For example, at work I have these dense policy reviews or long stretches of data analysis where I need to sit and really read carefully, compare details, think through implications, and not miss anything. And I find myself putting those off until later in the day, even when I know that’s probably the worst time to do them. It’s like the thought of sitting with that much detailed reading and thinking feels almost physically hard to start, like there’s this wall in front of it.

I’ll tell myself, “Okay, I just need a clear block of time,” or “I’ll do it after I answer these smaller emails,” and then suddenly it’s late afternoon and I still haven’t done the thing that required the most focus. And by then I’m already mentally worn down, so it takes even more effort to make myself begin. It’s frustrating because the work itself matters, and I’m capable of understanding it, but sustaining that level of attention for a long time feels draining in a way that’s disproportionate to just sitting at a desk.
